By the Associated Press


NEW YORK, September 20.--A kidnap band which restored 8-year-old John Arthur Russell to his wealthy father when the police hunt became too hot was sought throughout New York and many parts of the East today.


Stolen and held for $25,000 ransom, the boy was returned mysteriously late last night to the Brooklyn home of his father, Arthur S. Russell, Stock Exchange broker. Police announced no ransom was paid and that they believed the kidnappers had been frightened by an intense search.


Young Russell was so tired when he got home that police refrained from questioning him extensively until to-day. On his way home from school yesterday, he said, two men stopped him, took him for an auto ride and then to a small flat, where they gave him sandwiches, milk and a picture book.


In the evening, he said, a woman and another man came in, and the woman took him by automobile to a street car, gave the conductor a nickel and asked him to let the boy off near his home. Three telephone operators saw him get off the car, recognized him from his picture in a newspaper and took him home.


While the boy was missing, two telephone calls were received at the Russell home demanding $25,900 for the boy's safe return. Detectives expressed the belief the kidnapping was engineered by amateurs.

streets and highways is an extreme
ly hazardous practice. Whenever a
tire must be changed the car should
be moved wholly off the main tray
eled road, so that it will be out of
the line of traffic. This is especially
important if it is dark. If tire trou-
BILE does occur after dark the motor
ist will be fortunate if it happens
near a filling station or if there is a
well-lighted area into which he can
drive his car.


1t is always advisable, however,
to carry an electric flashlight or
trouble lamp which may be connect
ed to the lighting current in the
car, because puncture or blowout
may occur ON dark road far from
any source of artificial illumination.
In such case if the mOtorist is
wearing dark outer clothes and a
light colored shirt he should remove
his coat and vest before starting
work, because his shirt will be more
easily visible to drivers of ap-
preaching vehicles. He should leave
the lights burning on his car and

conceal it from view. Moreover, for
greater safety it would be advisable
to have one of the passengers hold
the fashlight and use it as warn
ing signal to approaching drivers.

adjacent to the highway should be
kept closed All tools, seat cushions,
spare tires and other objects should
be kept off the roadway. If stones or
pieces of timber are used for block
ing the wheels of the car they
should be moved to safe place at
the side of the road before the car
is driven away.

ought to have a fairly clear idea


what the law requires. If people
have only hazy idea about the law,
they are likely to violate it. One
reason why the laws and regula-
tons governing automobile opera
tion are so frequently violated, is
that these laws and regulations vary
so much in different states, and diff
ferent places in the same state.


These variations are so great that
many motorists who are ordinarily
law abiding, have reached the con-
clusion that the laws and regulations
are so complex that it is impossible
to obey them. So they do about as
they think is right.


Many communities add to the con-
fusion by warning signs erected
years ago which they never attempt
to enforce. 1t is rather common to
see signs on the outskirts of viii
lagos warning driving not to run
over Is or 20 miles an hour. Those
signs may have been erected years
before when the driving habits of
the people were different. The aver
age motorist, on seeing such a sign,
and noting that no one is in sight or
anywhere near, does not see any ne
cessity of obeying it. But when
once people get in the habit of ig-
noring the laws on such matters,
the habit of violating laws and or
dinances is strengthened.


In some states motorists may use
their own judgment in the way they
approach railroad crossings, while
in others they are required to stop
before crossing. Dimming of head
lights is required in some states and
not in others. There are many like
in the laws.

regulate traffic in accordance with
it's own local conditions. But it
would help get these necessary laws
if communities would en-
force the laws that they consider
necessary, and remove notices re-
quiring action that they do not pro-
pose to insist upon. Also if there
could be a movement to make the
laws of the states as nearly uniform
as possible.

The La Follette dynasty defends its throne against new foes.

He was to make his formal admission at a deportation hearing where immigration officials were to worry once more about their most persistent and embarrassing guest. They had deported his royal highness twice before. Each time he embarrassed them by returning right under their noses.

Last spring, while awaiting deportation, "Prince Mike" was permitted to go to Manhattan with a guard to get his clothes. He got the guard intoxicated in a speakeasy and escaped, but later was captured and deported.

His royal highness was arrested yesterday only week after his return to America. He was betrayed by his own regal tastes. He went into Dunhill, English tobacconist, to get his favorite mixture—Royal Yacht at $10 a pound.

Immigration officials had called at Dunhills and asked the manager to call a policeman should the prince appear. A policeman was called. Immigration officials, publicly refusing to believe, privately laid out the lines that brought his capture.

If he doesn't, he may be deported at the expense of the North German Lloyd Line provided it is proved that he stowaway away on the Europa. Washington -- Probably there is some great moral lesson in the story of what happened during the Chicago convention between Al Smith and William G. McAdoo and between Al Smith and Jack Garner.

If not, then it's just a tale of three slick politicians, a rather diverting tale of some of the undercover machinations which preceded the nomination of another politician who proved slicker than any of them.

What appears to be Smith's version of his dealings with McAdoo and Garner has been given by Frank K. Kent in the Baltimore Sun. It serves to explain the grim rage which possessed Al as he left Chicago after his failure to block Roosevelt, a rage which apparently possessed him for some months thereafter.

Roosevelt had a very large majority of delegates, but Smith, full of politeness, was a believer in the theory of majority stopping Roosevelt in favor of, in agreement with other leaders, "smoke-filled room" stuff.

He succeeded at blocking leading contenders for the nomination. He had carried the flag for the northern democratic bosses in 1924 when they used the two-thirds rule to break the favorite candidate of the west and the south. And his victim in that weird deadlock was none other than this same McAdoo, who then had plenty of support of the Ku Kluxers and even a spot or two of oil on him.

But in Roosevelt he now had a far tougher piece of meat to chew. McAdoo never quite did get a majority at Madison Square Garden, although he could have had it and would have won had it not been for the two-thirds rule.

Smith still disliked McAdoo at Chicago, but perhaps he didn't realize that McAdoo disliked Smith much more intensely. And Smith was willing to make a deal with his old victim because, as he told Bernard Baruch, who arranged the meeting, "In this fight I would sleep with a Chinaman to win." McAdoo held nearly 100 delegates for Garner, for the Texas delegates wouldn't break before he released his own Californians.

Then begins the story of willyness and guile.

Did Smith or McAdoo consider for a moment the thought that the millions of democratic primary voters and the hundreds of delegates picked by state conventions ought to have something to say about the nomination?

Was any thought given to popular government or the idea that Roosevelt's huge majority might mean that he was the party's real choice? Hardly.

Here were a couple of slick politicians.

Smith undertook to show how Roosevelt could be held for five ballots and then smashed.

From a flourishing industry that

rode through the depression period without any serious setbacks until last Spring, the business of broadcasting appears to have reached its lowest ebb in recent years. Happily for the broadcasters, however, and accordingly for the listening public—which gets better programs as more sponsors compete for its attention—the recession in the tide of radio business seems to have halted. Unless an unexpected new slump sets in, the broadcasting business can look forward to a new era of prosperity this Autumn and Winter.

Definite prospects that old sponsors will return to the air this Fall and that many new sponsors will give radio a fling have caused decided clearing of the blue atmosphere that has pervaded radio studios generally throughout the Summer. Every time an advertiser leaves the air it means just that much more expense for the broadcaster, who must then himself pay for sustaining talent in order to maintain his program schedule and hold listener interest.

Most Stations In Red.

The result has been rigorous curtailment of staffs and salaries in order to make ends meet. If program quality has fallen off during the Summer, it is simply because revenues have not warranted expenditures for new features. Only a handful of stations out of the 600 in the United States have operated in the black during the last few months.

How seriously the slump has hit radio in recent months is well indicated by network revenue figures, often regarded as an index to the broadcasting business as a whole. During July, the last month for which figures are available, the two nationwide chain organizations suffered the severest curtailment in income since 1930. NBC and CBS together crossed $2,406,228 during that month, which compares with $2,764,294 during July, 1931. It was the lowest month's revenue in 10 months, representing withdrawal, in many cases for the Summer only, of some of the leading sponsors of some of the most popular programs on the air. It was particularly hard for the networks to swallow, because they started the year 1932 with a bang, hanging up revenue records from January through May. The slump came in June.

Networks Show Gain.

Because of the good start they got during the first five months of this year the two network organizations can nevertheless show considerably higher income so far this year than during the same months of 1931. The figure for the first seven months of 1932 is $25,214,835; for the same months of 1931 it was $20,167,532. But the Summer slump has been so severe—it will be shown also in the August figures, not yet announced—that considerably more business will have to be done to equal last year's record revenue of $35,791,999. It is conservatively estimated that time sold by stations independently of their network connections, for which no tabulations are made, runs about twice that of network time, i. e., around $70,100,000 a year, so that the gross time turnover of American radio is well over $100,000,000 a year. Local stations have suffered business letdowns commensurately with the networks—in many cases, much more severely because of unusually depressed local industrial conditions.

The evidence that business is on the upgrade is furnished by the growing lists of new sponsors reported both by networks and local stations, as well as by the fact that many old sponsors are definitely arranging to return. All through the broadcasting industry, there runs a note of optimism. If the business of broadcasting can be regarded as an index to business conditions generally, then happier days are in store for American industry.

The transport problem is usu
ally viewed from two distinct
attitudes. One is that the rail
roadssare being unfairly treated
and that all common carriers
should be regulated as much
alike as is feasible. The other
is that the railroads are dying
industry and that there is no
point in cramping the style of
progress by extending strict
regulation to their competitors.
To many uniformed or un
thinking persons, this last areu
ment is persuasive one. We
see trucks carrying merchandise
and freight where, few years
ago, the railroads were supreme.
We see buses ply the highways
loaded with passengers that once
travelled by railroad. It's easy
to believe the dying industry

The figures, however, paint a

all freight tonnage. No other
medium has arisen that shows
any sign of being able to take
their place, particularly on long
hauls.


The problem, then, resolves
into this: We must have a
transport policy that recognizes
conditions as they are-not as
they we're or may be. There is

for airplanes. for waterways
but that doesn't mean that the

The railroads are and will con-

The transport problem is usually viewed from two distinct attitudes. One is that the railroads are being unfairly treated and that all common carriers should be regulated as much alike as is feasible. The other is that the railroads are dying industry and that there is no point in cramping the style of progress by extending strict regulation to their competitors. To many uninformed or unthinking persons, this last argument is a persuasive one. We see trucks carrying merchandise and freight where, few years ago, the railroads were supreme. We see buses ply the highways loaded with passengers that once travelled by railroad. It's easy to believe the dying industry argument.

The figures, however, paint a different story. The railroads still carry almost all the heavy tonnage of the country. They still move about 85 per cent of all freight tonnage. No other medium has arisen that shows any sign of being able to take their place, particularly on long hauls.

The problem, then, resolves into this: We must have a transport policy that recognizes conditions as they are—not as they were or may be. There is place for trucks, for pipelines, for airplanes, for waterways, but that doesn't mean that the railroads have been replaced. The railroads are and will continue to be the backbone of the nation's transport. That being true, any sound program must guarantee them a fair deal and allocate to each carrier its most useful place in the transport scheme.

THE PRESS


MILLEDGEVILLE, Ga., Nov. 5.
A father and son died in the electric chair here Friday afternoon, after the son attempted to shift all blame for a crime from his father to himself, and tried to kill himself.


The two were William Hulsey, whose last words were, "The Lord is with me; I am innocent," and his son Fred, who asked the prison chaplain to tell his father, "I will see you in heaven."


They were convicted of killing three men in a poker game on their farm at Rockhart, Ga., two years ago.


The suicide attempt occurred at the very hour that Governor Richard B. Russell Jr., who Thursday denied the doomed men a reprieve, was motoring through North Carolina from Raleigh to High Point for a campaign speech.


Superintendent B. N. Dunaway of the prison immediately advised Russell's young executive secretary, J. K. Hay, at Atlanta.


Holds Up Electrocutions


On his own responsibility—remembering that the state law provides for executions of death sentences between 10 a. m. and 2 p. m. of the date set—Hay instructed the superintendent to hold up action until he could talk to the young Governor. The electrocutions were postponed until 4 S.


If the Governor were not reached by 4 p. m., Hay said, he was inclined to let the electrocutions proceed, if physicians considered the condition of Fred Hulsey warranted.


Governor Russell telephoned to Hay at Atlanta and ordered a late physician's report on Hulsey's condition. Less than an hour before the legal deadline, the report came. The would-be suicide was in condition to go through with the ordeal, Dr. Richard Binion said. The secretary then gave the final order.


Young Hulsey was first to enter the death chamber, borne in the arms of a prison attendant and bleeding from his self-inflicted wounds.


Takes Fifteen Seconds


"God save me! Lord help me!"
The son cried as he was strapped in at 1:42 p. m. Six minutes later, after telling the chaplain he would "see father in heaven," the switch was thrown. Fifteen seconds later Fred Hulsey was dead, the quickest electrocution Dr. Binion said he ever saw.


An attendant washed the electric chair and the father was strapped to it at 1:53 p. m. Three minutes later the switch was thrown and left thrown for 33 seconds. The elder Hulsey was pronounced dead at 2:05 p. m. His last words were "Eyes, sir," in reply to the warden's question if he had anything more to say after declaring he was innocent.


The Hulseys and a group of neighbors got together one afternoon in July, 1930, for a rustic poker game in a field near the Hulsey farm home at Rockhart. There was home brew. The Hulseys lost money. A fight resulted in the shooting of Clifford Jones, Lige Harper and Ernest Mccullough.

An effort to get prompt action in
Congress looking to reorganization of
the Government departments by in
cluding in the Interior Department ap-
preparation bill an amendment con-
ferring broad reorganization power on
the President will be made by Senator
Vandenberg, Republican, of Michigan,
when the Senate resumes consideration
of the Interior bill this afternoon.


Senator Vandenberg will offer his
proposal while the Senate is consider
ing the provisions placed in the bill by
the House to prohibit salary promotions
and to curtail the filling of vacancies
until after July, 1888. These two limi-
,tations were advanced by the House as
economy measures. The Senate Ap-
preparations Committee has recon-
mended that they be eliminated from
this and other appropriation bills IN
order that further discussion of the ad-
visibility of such restrictions may oe
had in conference.


In Line With Georges Resolution.


Senator Vandenberg feels that since
the House has, by these limitations,
opened the door to discussion of per-
sonnel problems. that it would be ap-
propriate in that connection for the
Senate to consider steps looking to
general reorganization of governmental
agencies


Senator Vandenberg's proposal to
give the President authority to pro-
coed with reorganization of bureaus or
departments is in line with a resolution
prepared by Senator George, Democrat,
of Georgia, which has been favorabiy
reported to the Senate from the Fl
nance Committee. If the move to at
tach a reorganization plan to the In
terror appropriation bill succeeds, its
chances of enactment at this session
would be much greater than if it is
considered separately.


Howard U. Fight Up Again.


The Senate also will reach a final
determination this afternoon on the
question of how much should be allow
ed in the Interior bill for Howard Uni
yersity. Late yesterday afternoon the
Senate, on motion of Senst tor Smoot of
Utah, in charge of the bill, restored the
s$400,000 which the Appropriations
Committee had cut out, for the building
program at the university. Today SEN
ator Costigan, Democrat of Colorado,
will offer further amendments to put
back some OF the money for salaries
and general expenses of the university
which was recommended by the Budget
Bureau, but reduced by the House


While the House restrictions on sal
AIRY promotions and filling of vacancies
are at issue in the Interior bill, the final
decision on these questions will come in
the conference report on the agricul-
tural appropriation BILL since that is the
first bill to reach the conference stage.
Since Incorporating these limitations in
several of the early appropriation bills,
the House has partially reversed its stand
by leaving out of the Treasury-Po
Office bill the ban on normal salary
promotions. With regard to vacancies,
the House has provided in all the ap-
preparation bills that only such vacan-
cies as the President declares to be
essential may be filled.

LOS ANGELES, Nov. 5. U.P)-
Charges that a man and woman
lurked outside the home of Charles
H. Scull, wealthy engraver, several
days before he was killed were be-
fore Superior Court Judge Isaac
Pacht today, hearing evidence in
the murder trial of Libbie Olson,
and her husband, I. Albert Olson.


H. N. Barnett, a radio man, test
flied late yesterday that on two
occasions he saw a man and woman
prowling around the Scull home
late at night. He said he "be-
lieved" the man was Olson, but
could not identify him positively
because it was dark.


Barnett's testimony came after
the state, in trying to establish
that the Olsons killed Scull, their
friend, because they feared he
would cut them out of his will, re-
called the engraver's fiancee, Mrs.
Mildred Coons, to the stand. Mrs.
Coons, who lived next door to
Scull, said he murmured the single
word "Olson" a moment before he
died. Previously, Coons had testi-
fled that Barnett telephoned
him a few hours earlier at his
home where they were playing
cards.
